# Why the Night Is Dark

Here is a question that sounds like something a child would ask and that turns out to be one of the deepest questions a person can pose: why is the sky dark at night?

The obvious answer is that the sun has gone down. The sun is on the other side of the Earth, lighting up somebody else's afternoon, and so our half of the planet is in shadow. This is true, and it is also completely beside the point. The sun is only one star. There are others, a great many others, and the question is why all of *them*, taken together, do not light up the sky.

To feel the force of this, imagine standing in a forest. If the forest is small, you can see gaps between the trunks, patches of open field beyond. But if the forest is large enough, and the trees are scattered more or less evenly, then every line of sight you could possibly draw from where you stand will eventually hit a tree. Look in any direction and you see bark. There are no gaps. The forest has become a wall.

Now replace the trees with stars and the forest with the universe. If the universe goes on forever, and if stars are scattered through it more or less evenly, then every line of sight from your eye, in any direction you care to look, should eventually end on the surface of a star. There should be no gaps. The whole sky, every square degree of it, should be as bright as the surface of the sun. Not a pleasant evening glow. A blaze. The night sky should be a furnace.

It is not. It is dark, speckled with a few thousand visible points of light, and the darkness between them is the most ordinary thing in the world. We have been looking at it for as long as there have been eyes to look. And that ordinary darkness is a clue about the origin of everything.

---

The puzzle usually goes by the name of Olbers' paradox, after Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers, a German physician and astronomer who wrote about it in 1823. Like many things named after people, it was not really his. Johannes Kepler had raised a version of it two centuries earlier, in 1610, and used it as an argument that the universe must be finite, that the stars could not go on forever, because if they did the sky would be bright. Edmond Halley worried about it in the 1720s. A Swiss astronomer named Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux worked through it with real care in 1744, and calculated that an infinite, eternal, evenly starred universe would produce a sky tens of thousands of times brighter than the sun.

The argument can be made precise with a small piece of geometry. Imagine the universe divided into concentric shells around the Earth, like the layers of an onion, each shell the same thickness. A shell twice as far away has four times the surface area, so it contains roughly four times as many stars. But each of those stars, being twice as far away, appears only a quarter as bright. The two effects cancel exactly. Every shell, no matter how distant, contributes the same amount of light as every other shell. And if there are infinitely many shells, you are adding up the same finite amount of light infinitely many times.

In practice the sum doesn't quite run to infinity, because nearer stars block the light of farther ones, which is the forest-wall effect again. But the ceiling it runs into is still a sky as bright as a stellar surface, everywhere, all the time. You would not survive a night like that. Neither would the oceans.

What I love about this argument is how little it assumes. It doesn't require a telescope or a theory of gravity or any knowledge of what stars are made of. It requires only three premises: that the universe is infinite in extent, that it is filled roughly evenly with stars, and that it has been this way forever, or at least long enough for light to get around. From those premises and some schoolroom geometry, you derive a conclusion that is flatly contradicted by walking outside after dinner. So at least one of the premises must be wrong.

---

People tried a lot of escape routes.

One idea was that dust and gas between the stars absorb the distant light, dimming it before it reaches us. This sounds plausible. There *is* dust between the stars, and it *does* absorb light. But it doesn't solve the problem, and the reason is thermodynamic. If the dust absorbs starlight, it heats up. Given enough time, and an eternal universe offers unlimited time, the dust would heat until it glowed as brightly as the stars themselves. You cannot hide energy forever by soaking it up in a sponge. Eventually the sponge becomes a lamp.

Another idea was that the stars are not spread evenly but arranged hierarchically, clusters within clusters within clusters, in such a way that the density thins out fast enough at large scales for the sum to converge. This is mathematically possible, and some people took it seriously for a while. It has a certain elegance, a fractal universe with ever-larger voids. But it isn't what we observe. On the largest scales, the universe looks remarkably uniform.

Kepler's answer was the simplest: the universe is finite. There is an edge, and beyond the last stars there is nothing, a dark wall, and it is this wall we see between the stars. But an edge to space raises its own questions. What is on the other side? And as physics developed, a boundary wall in space started to look less and less like something nature would do.

---

The answer that turned out to be right came first, astonishingly, from a poet.

In 1848, the year before he died, Edgar Allan Poe published a long, strange, feverish prose poem called *Eureka*. It is a work of cosmology, or of something adjacent to cosmology, in which Poe tried to explain the entire structure of the universe from first principles. Much of it is wrong, and much of it is grandiose in a way that makes it hard to read now. But buried in it is this passage:

> Were the succession of stars endless, then the background of the sky would present us an uniform luminosity, like that displayed by the Galaxy, since there could be absolutely no point, in all that background, at which would not exist a star. The only mode, therefore, in which, under such a state of affairs, we could comprehend the voids which our telescopes find in innumerable directions, would be by supposing the distance of the invisible background so immense that no ray from it has yet been able to reach us at all.

Read that last sentence again. *No ray from it has yet been able to reach us at all.* Poe had spotted that the problem was not space but time. Light travels at a finite speed. If the universe, or at least its population of shining stars, has only existed for a finite amount of time, then we can only see light from stars close enough for their light to have arrived. Beyond that distance the stars may well exist, but their light is still in transit. We are, in effect, looking at a forest in which the trees beyond a certain distance haven't been planted yet, or rather, whose images haven't reached us yet.

This is essentially the modern resolution. Lord Kelvin worked out a quantitative version around 1901, and later the astronomer Edward Harrison argued at length, in a lovely book called *Darkness at Night*, that the finite age of the universe is the main reason the sky is dark. Stars don't burn long enough, and the universe hasn't existed long enough, for starlight to fill space to the brim. To reach the blazing wall of Olbers' imagination, you would need light traveling for vastly longer than the roughly 13.8 billion years the universe has been around, and vastly longer than any star can shine.

There is a second effect too, which Poe could not have known about: the universe is expanding. Light from distant galaxies is stretched as it travels, shifted toward the red, losing energy along the way. This dims the far-off contributions further. For a while the popular explanation of Olbers' paradox gave expansion the starring role, but most cosmologists now think Harrison was right that finite age does most of the work and expansion is a supporting player. Either way, the conclusion is the same, and it is extraordinary.

The darkness of the night sky is evidence that the universe had a beginning.

You don't need a particle accelerator or a space telescope to see it. You need to go outside on a clear night, away from the streetlights, and notice what's between the stars.

---

But the story has one more turn, and it's my favorite part.

It turns out that the sky *is* bright, everywhere, in every direction, just as Olbers' argument said it should be. We just can't see it.

In the early universe, everything was hot and dense, a glowing plasma of charged particles in which light couldn't travel far before being scattered. The universe was opaque, like the inside of a star, or like fog. Then, about 380,000 years after the beginning, it cooled enough, to a few thousand degrees, for electrons and protons to combine into neutral atoms. Suddenly light could travel freely. The fog lifted.

The light that was released at that moment is still traveling. It fills the whole universe. And when we look out into space, far enough in any direction, our line of sight eventually runs into that moment, the last moment when the universe was opaque. Beyond it, we cannot see, because the universe itself was a glowing wall.

So Olbers was right, in a way he never imagined. Every line of sight does end on a luminous surface. Look in any direction and, at the far end of your gaze, there is something glowing as hot as the surface of a star. It's just that the surface isn't made of stars. It's the universe itself, as it was when it was young.

The reason this wall doesn't blind us is expansion. In the 13.8 billion years since, the universe has stretched by a factor of about eleven hundred, and the light has stretched with it. What left as a yellow-orange glow at around three thousand degrees now arrives as microwaves, at a temperature of about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. The furnace is still there. It's been cooled to a whisper by the sheer amount of space that has opened up between us and it.

This is the cosmic microwave background, and its discovery in 1965 is one of the great stories of accidental science. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, were trying to use a large horn-shaped antenna and found an annoying hiss they couldn't get rid of. It came from every direction, day and night, regardless of season. They checked their equipment. They famously evicted a pair of pigeons that had been nesting in the antenna and cleaned out what they delicately called "white dielectric material." The hiss remained. It was, they eventually learned, the afterglow of the beginning of the universe.

Some of it, a small fraction, used to show up as the static on old analog televisions tuned between channels. People used to fall asleep in front of it. A little of the snow on the screen was light from the dawn of time, which is the sort of fact that seems like it ought to change how everyone lives, and somehow doesn't.

---

I keep coming back to this puzzle because of what it shows about how knowledge works.

The first thing it shows is that the most ordinary observations can carry the most information, if you ask the right question about them. The darkness of the night sky had been noticed by every human being who ever lived. It took an unusual kind of attention to see it as strange, to refuse the obvious answer ("the sun went down") and ask why the obvious answer was actually sufficient. Most of the time the familiar is invisible to us precisely because it's familiar. We explain it away before we've really looked at it. The paradox begins the moment someone declines to do that.

The second thing it shows is how a wrong answer can be half right. Kepler thought the dark sky meant the universe was finite in space. He was wrong about space but right that something had to be finite, and it turned out to be time. The hierarchical-universe people were wrong, but they were right that the uniform-infinite-eternal model had to break somewhere. Even Olbers' naive expectation, a sky uniformly ablaze, turned out to be literally true, only shifted into a part of the spectrum our eyes evolved to ignore. There is something humbling and hopeful in that. The first attempts to answer a hard question are rarely correct, but they are often pointing in a real direction.

The third thing, and maybe the one that moves me most, is Poe. Here is a man known for tales of premature burial and a talking raven, broke, grieving, a year from his death, writing a cosmology that most scientists of his day ignored and that is mostly wrong, and in the middle of it he gets the single most important part of this problem right. He didn't have the math. He didn't have the physics. He had a question he couldn't stop turning over and the willingness to follow it somewhere uncomfortable, all the way to the idea that there is a horizon to what we can see, set not by where things stop but by how long there has been for light to travel.

I don't think this means intuition beats rigor. Kelvin's calculation mattered. Harrison's careful accounting of energy mattered. Penzias and Wilson's patient elimination of every mundane explanation, pigeons included, mattered enormously. Poe's guess was a guess, and he made plenty of other guesses in the same book that went nowhere. But it does suggest that the space of good ideas is not fenced off by credentials, and that a mind willing to take a simple question with total seriousness can sometimes get further than it has any right to.

---

There is a last thought I want to leave here, a small and personal one.

When you look up on a dark night, you are seeing a kind of history. The nearby stars show you light that left them years or centuries ago. The faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy, if you can find it, shows you light that left before there were humans. And the darkness between everything, that plain black background, is itself a message: that there was a beginning, that time is finite looking backward, that there hasn't been enough of it for the light to fill the sky. Beyond the darkness, invisible to us but measurable with the right instruments, is the glow of the beginning itself, stretched thin and cold across billions of years, still arriving, still faintly warm.

It's easy to think of the night as an absence, the thing that happens when the light goes away. But the darkness is doing something. It's holding information. It's telling us how old everything is. The black between the stars is not nothing; it's the shape of time made visible, the edge of what has had a chance to reach us so far.

I find that consoling in a way I can't entirely explain. Maybe it's that the universe turns out to be legible: not simple, not obvious, but readable, if you're patient and willing to be surprised. The answer to a child's question was written across the sky the whole time. We only had to learn how to read it, and the reading took a physician, a poet, a physicist, two radio astronomers, and some pigeons.

The next time you're somewhere truly dark, look up and notice the black. It's been waiting a long time for someone to find it strange.
